extracted.intended_audience: Royal Society fellows, experimental natural philosophers, and instrument makers (optics)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural guidance and evaluation criteria for prismatic colour experiments (reconstituting white light) and for building/testing early reflecting telescopes and their metalline specula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prism–lens whiteness-reconstitution experiment setup
rubrics_metrics.description: In a darkened room make a hole in the shut of a window (diameter about a third part of an inch) to admit sun-light; place a clear and colourless prism to refract the entering light; place a lens of about three feet radius at a distance of about four or five feet so the refracted colours convene at about ten or twelve feet; intercept the light at that distance with a sheet of white paper to see the colours converted into whiteness again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the prism and lens are placed steady; move the paper to and fro to find the distance at which whiteness is most perfect and to observe how the colours gradually convene, vanish into whiteness, cross, and afterwards are dissipated and severed in inverted order. If any of the colours at the lens are intercepted, the whiteness will be changed into other colours; therefore care must be taken that none of the colours fall beside the lens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of motion to locate optimal focus and observe colour intermixture
rubrics_metrics.description: Move the paper on which the colours are projected to and fro to determine the distance where whiteness is most perfect and to observe the progressive mingling and separation of prismatic colours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By motion you will see at what distance the whiteness is most perfect, how the colours gradually convene and vanish into whiteness, and how, after crossing one another where they compound whiteness, they are again dissipated and retain the same colours in inverted order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark-room requirement and control of stray/scattering light
rubrics_metrics.description: For trials intended to test uncompounded colours (e.g., impossibility of changing an uncompounded colour), the room must be made very dark to prevent scattering light from mixing with the colour and rendering it compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A very dark room is requisite; otherwise scattering light will disturb and allay the colour and render it compound, contrary to the design. Perfecter separation of the colours than that produced by a single prism may be needed; where colours are not thoroughly separated, allow for changes proportionable to the mixture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation/controls when intercepting a prismatic colour
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prismatic colour (for example red) is to be intercepted to test whether it can be reproduced from the others, either the colours must be very well parted before interception, or the neighbouring colours (into which any red is secretly dispersed) must also be intercepted, or allowances must be made for any red emerging from yellow/green.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If these precautions are observed (thorough separation or interception including neighboring colours), then new production of the intercepted colour will be found impossible. If not, apparent reproduction may be due to residual dispersion of that colour into neighboring bands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for imperfect separation of colours
rubrics_metrics.description: When trials are made with colours not thoroughly separated, changes in appearance must be allowed proportionable to the mixture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: compound yellow light falling upon blue bise will not appear perfectly yellow but rather green, because yellow mixture contains many rays indued with green which are more copiously reflected by the blue bise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflecting telescope basic optical configuration
rubrics_metrics.description: The new instrument is composed of two metalline specula (one concave, the other flat/plain) and a small plano-convex eye-glass; the tube is open at the object end, closed where the concave is laid, with a flat oval speculum fixed near the open end inclined towards the upper tube where a hole with the eye-glass permits viewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rays from the object fall on the concave at the bottom, are reflected toward the flat speculum, and by reflection are directed to the small eye-glass and to the spectator's eye. The flat speculum is made as small as possible to avoid obstructing entrance rays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimensional proportions and magnification calculation for the reflecting telescope
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific dimensions and focal relations: concave speculum radius about 12½ or 13 inches; small eye-glass radius about 1/12 of an inch; ratio of focal distances EF to ETV given as 1 to 38, yielding approximate magnification of 38 times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare distances of focus from vertices of the little eye-glass and concave speculum to estimate magnification. Experimental checks (e.g., observing a distant crown on a weather-cock or reading print at 100–120 feet) are recommended to judge instrument performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment requirement for flat speculum
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of the flat speculum must be placed in the same point of the tube's axis where falls the perpendicular drawn to the same from the centre of the little eye-glass (point marked T).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper alignment of the flat speculum on the tube axis is necessary so that reflected rays are correctly directed to the eye-glass and yield a distinct image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material selection: avoid porous metalline compositions for specula
rubrics_metrics.description: For a fit metalline substance do not use one full of small pores (discoverable by microscope); though such metal may initially take a good polish, pores' edges wear away faster during polishing and prevent accurate regular reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fumes raised in fusion (e.g., from tin glass mixed with bell metal) can fill metal with microscopical pores; white arsenic both blanches the metal and leaves it solid without such pores (if fusion not too violent). Examine metal throughout for porosity before judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alloy proportions and melting/casting procedure for specula
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested proportions: arsenic between a sixth and eighth part by weight of the copper; example mixes include arsenic 1 oz, copper 6 oz, tin 2 oz; excessive arsenic makes metal brittle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Melting procedure: melt the copper alone, then add arsenic (mind pernicious fumes), stir a little, then add tin and stir, and immediately pour off. Avoid too violent or prolonged fusion which may make the metal porous. Small admixtures of silver may whiten but soften metal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polishing technique and avoidance of fretting-induced pores
rubrics_metrics.description: Polishing powders (putty or similar) with sharp angular particles will fret the metal if not very fine and fill it with small holes; therefore care must be taken in choice and fineness of polishing grit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use very fine polishing materials; inspect for pores (microscopic) after polishing; verify the metal is solid throughout rather than merely appearing polished on the surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting and surface-quality inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: Instrument quality depends on composition and casting; visible defects like scabrous places or irregular figure impair representation (distinctness and freedom from colours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect for scabrous spots, uneven figure, or tarnish. Instruments with such imperfections are capable of further improvement; any observed defects indicate need for better casting/polishing or change in alloy composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical testing criteria for telescope goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge an instrument by practical trials such as reading printed text at large distances (e.g., reading a journal in sunlight at 100 feet, discerning some words at 120 feet) and by comparing with ordinary telescopes of known magnification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure aperture near the eye and compare magnification and distinctness with conventional instruments (e.g., 6-foot telescope). Note both magnification and resolution (distinctness, absence of colour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aiming/finding aids for high-magnification tubes
rubrics_metrics.description: High-magnification tubes make locating objects difficult; this is common to all tubes that magnify much.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies include affixing two sights to the iron rod that sustains the tube or attaching an ordinary perspective glass to the same frame, directed toward the same object, to assist in finding objects (as Descartes described).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric form consideration: parabolic vs spherical specula
rubrics_metrics.description: A parabolical speculum would have advantages over a spherical one in this construction, but working non-spherical surfaces with sufficient exactness is very difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although parabolical shapes may be preferable for reducing certain aberrations, practical manufacture may require mechanical devices or may be impracticable; spherical surfaces remain the pragmatic choice pending better grinding methods.
